choices: Eckmann–Hilton: an $n$-fold loop space carries two compatible compositions, and any two unital compositions sharing an interchange law agree and are commutative
Because the fundamental group always equals the higher homotopy groups
questions.explain: $\pi_n(X,x_0)=\pi_0(\Omega^n X)$, and $\Omega^n X$ for $n\ge 2$ is a $(n-1)$-fold loop space — it carries two compositions (loop in the $i$-th and $j$-th coordinates) which interchange, so by Eckmann–Hilton they coincide and are commutative.

questions.q: Compute $\pi_3(S^2)$. (Enter the rank as an integer; the group is $\mathbb{Z}^r$ — give $r$.)
questions.explain: $\pi_3(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the Hopf class $\eta$. The long exact sequence of the Hopf fibration $S^1\to S^3\to S^2$ together with $\pi_3(S^3)=\mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_3(S^1)=0$ gives the iso. Rank $1$.

questions.q: For a Serre fibration $F\to E\to B$ of pointed spaces, the long exact sequence of homotopy groups looks like:
choices: There is no general long exact sequence; this is fibration-specific
questions.explain: The fibration LES connects fibre / total space / base in homotopy: $\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\to\pi_n(E)\to\pi_n(B)\to\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots$, terminating at $\pi_0$. The connecting map $\partial$ comes from the path-lifting property of a Serre fibration.

questions.q: The Hurewicz theorem states that for an $(n-1)$-connected space $X$ with $n\ge 2$, the map $h\colon\pi_n(X)\to H_n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is:
choices: An isomorphism — the first non-trivial homotopy group equals the first non-trivial homology group
An isomorphism modulo the commutator subgroup, with no further hypothesis on $n$
questions.explain: For $X$ with $\pi_i=0$ for $i \lt n$ and $n\ge 2$, Hurewicz gives $h\colon\pi_n(X)\xrightarrow{\sim}H_n(X;\mathbb{Z})$. For $n=1$ the map is abelianisation $\pi_1\to H_1$ — surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup.

questions.q: The Whitehead theorem says a continuous map $f\colon X\to Y$ inducing isomorphisms $f_*\colon\pi_n(X)\to\pi_n(Y)$ for every $n$ is a homotopy equivalence — under what hypothesis?
choices: $X$ and $Y$ are connected CW complexes (or have the homotopy type of CW complexes)
$X$ and $Y$ are simply connected; no further hypothesis needed
questions.explain: The Whitehead theorem fails for general topological spaces: the Warsaw circle and a point have isomorphic (trivial) homotopy groups but are not homotopy equivalent. The CW hypothesis is the standard fix; for arbitrary spaces, use weak equivalence and CW-replacement.

questions.q: Which statements about Hurewicz and Whitehead are correct? Select all.
choices: If $X$ is simply connected and $H_n(X;\mathbb{Z})=0$ for all $n>0$, then $X$ is contractible — provided $X$ is a CW complex
Every map $f$ inducing an iso on $\pi_n$ for all $n$ is automatically a homeomorphism
Hurewicz fails in degree $1$: $\pi_1\to H_1$ is not an isomorphism in general; it is the abelianisation
Hurewicz applies in degree $n$ requiring only that $X$ be $(n-1)$-connected, not simply connected for higher $n$
questions.explain: Hurewicz + Whitehead jointly imply: a simply-connected CW complex with vanishing reduced homology is contractible. Hurewicz in degree 1 gives only abelianisation. Hurewicz in degree $n$ needs $(n-1)$-connectivity. But a homotopy equivalence is not the same as a homeomorphism — option 2 is wrong.

questions.q: What characterises an Eilenberg–MacLane space $K(G,n)$ up to homotopy equivalence?
choices: It is a finite-dimensional CW complex
questions.explain: An Eilenberg–MacLane space concentrates all homotopy in a single degree: $\pi_n=G$ and $\pi_k=0$ otherwise. For a fixed pair $(G,n)$ with $n\ge 1$ ($G$ abelian if $n\ge 2$) such a space exists and is unique up to homotopy equivalence — built by Postnikov / Whitehead tower constructions.

questions.q: The Brown representability statement for ordinary cohomology with coefficients in $G$ is:
choices: $H^n(X;G)\cong[X,K(G,n)]$ — the homotopy classes of maps from $X$ to $K(G,n)$
questions.explain: $K(G,n)$ represents singular cohomology in degree $n$ with coefficients $G$: there is a natural bijection $H^n(X;G)\cong[X,K(G,n)]$ for every CW complex $X$. Cohomology operations correspond to maps $K(G,n)\to K(H,m)$.

questions.q: Which of these are standard models for Eilenberg–MacLane spaces?
questions.explain: The first three are standard. $K(\mathbb{Z},n)\ne S^n$ in general: $S^n$ has rich higher homotopy (e.g. $\pi_3(S^2)=\mathbb{Z}$), while $K(\mathbb{Z},n)$ has homotopy concentrated in degree $n$. Only $S^1=K(\mathbb{Z},1)$ is itself a sphere.

questions.q: The Freudenthal suspension theorem states that $\Sigma\colon\pi_k(S^n)\to\pi_{k+1}(S^{n+1})$ is an isomorphism in what range?
choices: For every $k$ and $n$ — suspension is always an iso
questions.explain: Freudenthal: suspension is an iso for $k<2n-1$ and a surjection for $k=2n-1$. So $\pi_{n+k}(S^n)$ stabilises in $n$ for fixed $k$ once $n>k+1$ — defining the stable homotopy groups of spheres $\pi_k^s$.

questions.q: A spectrum is the data of:
choices: A single topological space $E$ with multiplication
A sequence of pointed spaces $\{E_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ together with structure maps $\Sigma E_n\to E_{n+1}$
An abelian group with a chain complex structure
A simplicial set with Kan extension
questions.explain: A (sequential) spectrum is $\{E_n,\sigma_n\colon\Sigma E_n\to E_{n+1}\}$. Examples: $H\mathbb{Z}$ with $E_n=K(\mathbb{Z},n)$ and $\sigma_n$ the Hurewicz map; the sphere spectrum $\mathbb{S}$ with $E_n=S^n$. Spectra represent generalised cohomology theories via $E^n(X)=[X,E_n]$.

questions.q: Which of the following are spectra (i.e. examples of generalised cohomology theories)?
choices: The Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum $H\mathbb{Z}$, representing singular cohomology with $\mathbb{Z}$-coefficients
The Thom spectrum $MO$, representing unoriented cobordism
The complex K-theory spectrum $KU$, representing topological complex K-theory
questions.explain: $H\mathbb{Z}$, $MO$, $KU$ are canonical spectra. A bare discrete space like $\mathbb{Z}$ does not carry the structure maps $\Sigma E_n\to E_{n+1}$; you would suspend it (giving the Moore spectrum $S\mathbb{Z}=H\mathbb{Z}$), but $\mathbb{Z}$ itself is not a spectrum.

questions.q: The Hopf fibration is which fibre sequence of spheres?
questions.explain: The classical Hopf fibration is $S^1\hookrightarrow S^3\to S^2$, viewing $S^3\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ and the projection to $\mathbb{CP}^1=S^2$. Its homotopy class generates $\pi_3(S^2)=\mathbb{Z}$. (There are also Hopf fibrations $S^3\to S^7\to S^4$ from $\mathbb{H}$ and $S^7\to S^{15}\to S^8$ from $\mathbb{O}$, but the classical one is the $S^1$-fibration.)

questions.q: What is $\dim_{\mathbb{Q}}\pi_3(S^2)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$? (Serre's rational homotopy of even-dim spheres.)
questions.explain: Serre's calculation: $\pi_*(S^{2n})\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ in degrees $2n$ and $4n-1$ and $0$ elsewhere. For $S^2$ ($n=1$), the non-zero degrees are $2$ and $3$, each of dimension $1$. So $\dim\pi_3(S^2)\otimes\mathbb{Q}=1$ — the Hopf class survives rationally.

questions.q: Sullivan's rational homotopy theory says that the $\mathbb{Q}$-homotopy type of a simply connected space of finite $\mathbb{Q}$-type is encoded by what algebraic gadget?
choices: A single chain complex of vector spaces
A minimal Sullivan model — a free commutative graded differential algebra (cdga) over $\mathbb{Q}$ quasi-isomorphic to $\Omega^*(X;\mathbb{Q})$
A spectral sequence with a $d_2$ differential
questions.explain: Sullivan: the rational homotopy category of simply-connected spaces of finite $\mathbb{Q}$-type is equivalent to the homotopy category of minimal Sullivan models — free graded-commutative dgas $(\Lambda V,d)$ with decomposable differential. The generators $V^n$ recover $\pi_n(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ dually.

questions.q: For a pointed space $X$, the based loop space $\Omega X$ satisfies which homotopy-group identity?
questions.explain: $\Omega X = \mathrm{Map}_*(S^1,X)$ shifts homotopy groups down: a map $S^n\to\Omega X$ adjoints to $S^n\wedge S^1=S^{n+1}\to X$, so $\pi_n(\Omega X)=[S^n,\Omega X]_*=[S^{n+1},X]_*=\pi_{n+1}(X)$.

questions.q: Bott periodicity for the stable unitary group $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{colim}\,\mathrm{U}(n)$ states:
questions.explain: Bott: $\Omega^2\mathrm{U}\simeq\mathrm{U}$, equivalently $\Omega(\mathbb{Z}\times B\mathrm{U})\simeq\mathrm{U}$, giving $\pi_n\mathrm{U}$ periodic of period $2$: $0,\mathbb{Z},0,\mathbb{Z},\ldots$ starting at $n=0$ (since $\mathrm{U}$ is connected). The stable orthogonal group has $8$-periodicity instead: $\Omega^8\mathrm{O}\simeq\mathrm{O}$.

questions.q: What is the period of the homotopy groups of the stable orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}$?
questions.explain: Bott periodicity for $\mathrm{O}$: $\pi_n\mathrm{O}$ is $8$-periodic, with values $\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2,0,\mathbb{Z},0,0,0,\mathbb{Z}$ in degrees $0,\ldots,7$. This $8$-fold periodicity drives the structure of real $K$-theory $KO$.
